"The intelligence ombudspersons consider that there are currently no newly emerged significant factual circumstances that would provide grounds for initiating an investigation," Justas Gaidys, senior adviser at the office, said in a comment to BNS. Gaudys said the decision not to investigate was based primarily on the fact that the parliamentary Committee on National Security and Defence (NSGK) had already carried out an inquiry into the alleged prison more than a decade ago on the instruction of the Seimas. He also noted that the Prosecutor General's Office is continuing a reopened pre-trial investigation and that the European Court of Human Rights (ECHR) has already delivered three judgments concerning the detention of individuals at alleged CIA facilities in Lithuania. "Recognising that this issue remains significant to the public, the Ombudsperson plans to initiate an inter-agency dialogue with the competent Lithuanian authorities," Gaidys said. "The aim of this dialogue will be to assess the possibilities of obtaining new information, determine whether any additional action falls within the ombudspersons' remit, and build a comprehensive understanding of the situation," he added. Debate over the alleged CIA prison resurfaced after Lithuania lost its third case before the ECHR in July. The Strasbourg court awarded 30,000 euros to Saudi Arabian national Abd Al Rahim Hussein Al-Nashiri over his unlawful detention at a secret CIA prison in Lithuania. The court also ordered the Lithuanian authorities to seek assurances from Washington that the terrorism suspect would not face the death penalty. Allegations that the CIA operated a secret detention facility in Lithuania first emerged in 2009, when US broadcaster ABC News reported that eight terrorism suspects had been held near Vilnius between 2004 and 2005. Later that year, the Seimas Committee on National Security and Defence (NSGK) concluded that it could not establish whether detainees had been transferred to Lithuania, but found that the conditions for such transfers had existed. Earlier this year, the Prosecutor General's Office confirmed that it is continuing its investigation into the alleged unlawful transportation of people across Lithuania's state border. Any further probe should be handled by an inter-agency commission, she added. "An inter-agency commission should investigate, if we were to form one. [...] We need to decide who actually has the competence to investigate and present arguments in a way that leaves no doubt in the future," TamaÅ¡unienÄ told reporters on Wednesday. https://www.hindustantimes.com/india-new.text: Poland is on India's side when it comes to fighting terrorism because "we are victim" of it, Polish envoy Piotr Antoni Switalski has said, asserting that his country supports India's "right to pursue terrorists everywhere they go".In his response to a query during a press interaction after an event on Thursday, Switalski, however, did not elaborate on his comments.Earlier in his address at an event hosted by the Centre for Integrated and Holistic Studies, the envoy said that Poland sees India as a very "effective partner", and the two countries can do things together, especially when the world has become a very unpredictable place, and there are "many disruptive forces"."We can build really an axis of stability, predictability, and good model for the global governance" and send a "good signal" to the outside world by doing good things together, he added. India-Poland cultural tiesThe Polish ambassador to India also underlined the cultural ties between the two countries, and mentioned the benevolent roles played by the then Maharaja Jam Sahib of Nawanagar, Sir Digvijaysinhji Ranjitsinhji Jadeja, who had sheltered Polish children during the World War II.He is known in Poland as the "Good Maharaja" and there is a Good Maharaja Square in Warsaw."He is a very emotional factor which makes for India, a special place in our hearts, the hearts of Poles," the envoy said. Switalski also spoke of a museum coming up in Kolhapur to mark the benevolent act of the then royal family of Kolhapur, which was at the forefront of giving shelter to Polish women and children displaced due to the horrors of World War II.Between 1942 and 1948, around 5,000 Polish refugees found shelter in Valivade, near Kolhapur, after being displaced by the tragedy of the Second World War.The settlement grew into a vibrant 'Little Poland', complete with schools, a church, and community life, offering hope and dignity to families far from their homeland, the Polish embassy had said in a social media post in June.In 2019, a memorial pillar was unveiled and the foundation for a museum was laid to preserve the memory of the Polish refugees who lived in Valivade.The museum is now nearing completion and ready to serve as a place where members of the Polish diaspora can reconnect with their family histories and the remarkable legacy of India's humanitarian spirit, it said.Poland sees India as defence partnerThe envoy said Poland is spending billions of euros on procurement, "and, we see India as a very attractive partner" because in some areas of defence production, India is very advanced and it has the scale.‘We support your right to pursue terrorists’Later, interacting with reporters, he said, "on the question of terrorism, we are on your (India's) side, because we are victim of terrorists"."You cannot compare, because the terrorist acts committed on Indian soil in the past years, including in Kashmir in 2025, were terrible. Nothing comparable happened in Poland. But we are on your side, and our voice, we said openly, we support your right to pursue terrorists everywhere they go. Because our policy on that is very clear. And we said it openly," the envoy said.On reports that Polish drones were used against Pakistani infrastructure in the first days and hours of Operation Sindoor, he said, there were reports by Indian sources, but also Pakistani sources."They shot down some of them, some of the drones, Polish drones," he said, adding that he suspected that they were "simply used as decoys, and they were training drones, and this is what experts were telling."The envoy said when he hears any statement using the Pakistani factor to attack Poland, "I'm really very surprised. And I suspect sometimes, a kind of foreign agenda behind it."Poland eyes wider economic cooperationIn his address, he also said Poland sees India as a "very effective partner" and is ready to work with it in agriculture and other fields, and "our companies are ready to work with you.""Some of the Indian companies are investing and operating in Poland. And I'm very glad, because Poland should be considered by your companies, as a friendly gateway to the European Union, to its big market, half a billion consumers," he said.He underlined that Poland and India may have a great asymmetry in terms of their sizes, and separated by thousands of miles, with rivers, seas, oceans, mountains, deserts, separating them."But, as we know, geography is a superficial measure of distance. As they say, true closeness is measured by the mind, the spirit, and the tongue. And I want to take you on a journey that reveals that Poland and India are not distant strangers, but ancient structural cousins, bound by a profound historical and emotional architecture," the envoy said.He underscored how the Polish language uses words which have roots in Sanskrit, and added that even his surname has Sanskrit roots."When Poland and India are looking at each other, we are looking into a mirror," he said."We can do things together, in times when the world has become a very unpredictable place, where the situation is quite turbulent, where you have so many disruptive forces. When you look at India and Europe, and Poland in particular, you can see that we can build really an axis of stability, predictability, and a good model for global governance," the envoy said."And that's probably why our relationship… When I say Poland, I mean also the European Union, is much more important than simply bilateral dimension. We can send a good signal to the outside world, by doing good things together," he said.

Photograph: Ana Escobar/EPA Weather tracker Spain Analysis Weather tracker: Thunderstorms hit Spain as Japan braces for typhoon James Michelin for MetDesk At least one person dead as stormy weather causes severe flooding in Barcelona and Valencia Fri 18 Sep 2026 04.36 EDT Last modified on Fri 18 Sep 2026 06.22 EDT Share Intense and slow-moving thunderstorms broke out on Wednesday afternoon across parts of eastern Spain, bringing some severe flooding and killing at least one person . Storms first struck over the Castilla-La Mancha region during the afternoon before passing over Spain’s east coast, becoming very slow-moving and continuing overnight. Torrential rainfall, strong winds and large hail were reported in Valencia and Barcelona, causing widespread flooding in both cities. Weather stations west of Barcelona recorded some of the highest totals with more than 100mm (4in) of rain falling in the space of a few hours, and locally 70mm in just 30 minutes in the early hours of Thursday morning. Cars and roads were submerged, and flights were cancelled across the region. Wednesday’s La Liga fixture between Levante and Athletic Club had to be postponed due to flooding at the Estadio Ciudad de Valencia. On Thursday rescuers found the body of a man near Olivella, west of Barcelona, after his car was swept away in the waters. Spain’s east coast is susceptible to extreme rainfall during the autumn months, as experienced in 2024, when devastating flash floods killed more than 200 people in Valencia . With the Mediterranean Sea reaching record temperatures, this is providing extra fuel and moisture to thunderstorms, making flooding more likely. In New Jersey in the US on Sunday, the Racefaster half marathon was disrupted due to extreme rainfall and a partly submerged course. Runners had to wade through chest-deep waters at times as 50mm-100mm of rain fell. Despite the flooding, 250 people managed to finish the race. Flooding was also reported to the north-east in Connecticut and Rhode Island, where up to 190mm of rain was recorded in a 36-hour period. Tropical Storm Dujuan, currently over the open west Pacific Ocean, will move north-west on a track towards Japan over the coming days. It is forecast to intensify into a category one typhoon on Friday. The joint typhoon warning centre is forecasting that Dujuan will skirt past the south-east coast of Japan, potentially affecting Tokyo and the surrounding areas. https://www.politico.eu/article/vladimir.text: President Vladimir Putin’s United Russia party secured a majority in the State Duma, Russia’s lower house, following the country’s first parliamentary elections since Moscow’s full-scale invasion of Ukraine began in 2022. In a widely expected result, the ruling party won around 58% of the vote for the 225 deputies elected via party lists, according to preliminary data from Russia’s Central Election Committee. Another 225 will be elected in single-mandate seats, where United Russia candidates are also dominating. Voting took place over the course of three days, with polls closing Sunday evening. The EU’s foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas said the elections “marked another major setback for Russian democracy” and their outcome “was never in doubt.” Advertisement Advertisement “I have proposed measures against those facilitating these sham elections in occupied Ukrainian territories,” she added. Residents of Donetsk, Luhansk, Zaporizhzhia and Kherson — regions that the Kremlin unlawfully occupied after the 2022 assault started — also took part in the vote, with some reportedly coerced into doing so . The war in Ukraine featured heavily in the elections , which were marked by severe repression. Dissenting voices were all but silenced, and Yabloko — the country’s only openly anti-war party — was banned from fielding a national list of candidates in the State Duma. “A party that has not been represented in the country’s parliament for 23 years [would have] secured second place in the polls, given the conditions in which we operate,” said Yabloko leader Nikolai Rybakov following the elections . “And the authorities could do nothing about it other than remove the party from the election.” Former Russian President Dmitry Medvedev, the deputy chairman of Russia’s Security Council, said of the results : “The citizens of our country maintain their trust in our leading political force [Putin’s party] and consider it appropriate to continue entrusting it with governance at various levels of state authority.”
